name: Захист від мату: зустрічний шах
description:
Counterattacks can be a fun and effective way of defending. But what good is a counterattack if you lose on the next turn?

Your opponent won’t mind losing a queen or a rook. Because he wins the game! Checkmate is more important than who has the most points.

Yet, sometimes a counterattact can be useful to prevent mate. You launch a counterattack on the king: check! This is called counter checking.

Your opponent has no time to checkmate your king. First, he needs to save his own king! Afterwards, things can be very different on the board. You might be able to escape checkmate now.

Have a look at the examples. The situation seems hopeless to White. He has no means of defending against mate. But he can, after a counter check.

Example 1: after counter checking White can protect the mating square.
Exampe 2 is slightly different. Wit launches a cunning couter check. In the next move he can capture the attacker.
In example 3, White is able to defend by interposing after his counter check.
Finally, example 4. This is a pretty difficult example. But it is a real fun one! See for yourself. Cool, huh?

It is not easy to come up with such tricks in a real game. That is why we are going to practise counter checking. How cool would it be if you could manage to escape mate in this way!

What do you have to do?
Defend against mate by counter checking. Then, continue defending by means of capturing, protecting, blocking or moving away.

examples.pgn: {[%csl Gg2][%cal Gh3g2]} 1. Qc4+ Kh8 {[%cal Gc4f1]} 2. Qf1 *
examples.text:
The black queen wants to checkmate on the green square.
There is nothing White can do to prevent that… except counter checking with his queen.

He moves his queen to right beneath the black pawn.
Now, Black cannot mate.
He needs to get out of check first. The black king flees.
From her new spot, the White queen can protect the mating square.

examples.pgn: {[%csl Gg2][%cal Gh3g2]} 1. Qb3+ {[%csl Rf3,Rg8]} Kh8 2. Qxf3 *
examples.text:
Again, Black plans on giving checkmate with the queen on the green square.

White can put the king in check, while at te same time attacking the bishop. This is called a double attack (but more about that later).
The black king moves out of check.
Now, White can defend by capturing.
The queen takes the bishop, an important attacker.
No checkmate.

examples.pgn: {[%csl Gc1][%cal Gc5c1]} 1. Bf6+ Kg8 {[%cal Gf6b2]} 2. Bb2 *
examples.text:
White has few options. Whatever he does, mate always seems to be the outcome: Black’s rook moves next to the king, where it is defended by the bishop.

There is only one thing White can do: give check with his bishop.
Black has to move his king into safety.
Of course, checkmate for White is still around the corner.
But now, White can defend his king.
He moves his bishop in between the black bishop and the mating square.
The attack is blocked and White is safe!

examples.pgn: {[%csl Gf1][%cal Gf3f1]} 1. Rg7+ Kh4 2. Kh1 {[%cal Gg7g1]} Rf1+ 3. Rg1 *
examples.text:
The black rook wants to give checkmate on the green square. White counter checks with his rook.
The black king has to step aside.
That is good news for White. He moves his king into the corner square.

How does that help? Black can still move his rook to the first rank…
Yes, but now White can defend himself! He puts his own rook between the king and the black rook. Wow!

texts: Defend against the mate threat. Use the black king's position.
